summary: Defines a simple string encoding of Presentation Addresses for environments where a text form is useful. It is informational.

eli5.summary: It is a way to write a computer address as plain text.

questions: what is the string encoding of presentation address
how to write an osi presentation address as a string
what are macros in presentation address strings
subtitle: A plain-text way to write down an OSI presentation address so people can read and type it.

tldr.problem: OSI presentation addresses are normally stored as ASN.1 structures, which people cannot easily read, type or print.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1278 defines a string syntax: optional selectors separated by slashes, followed by one or more network addresses joined with underscores.
tldr.outcome: The format is meant for display to system managers, not for internal storage. It is an Informational memo and says nothing about security.

facts.label: Address types (afi)
facts.value: X121, DCC, TELEX, PSTN, ISDN, ICD, LOCAL

today: RFC 1278 is an Informational memo, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes a display format tied to OSI presentation addresses.

sections.title: Why a String Form
sections.content:
OSI Application Entities use presentation addresses to find other Application Entities. Logically, a presentation address has a presentation selector, a session selector, a transport selector and a set of network addresses. The selectors are octet strings that often have IA5 character representations.

The OSI Directory stores these addresses using an ASN.1 representation. RFC 1278 adds a string encoding for the many contexts that need one. It is for display to human users, typically system managers rather than end users, and the RFC says it is not intended for internal storage. It was agreed as a unified syntax for the THORN and ISODE projects and is used throughout ISODE.
sections.eli5: A machine address is stored as a tangled bundle of data. This memo gives a way to write it as ordinary text so a person can read it.

sections.title: What the Format Must Do
sections.content:
The format must be able to specify any legal value, and must handle selectors in four encodings: IA5, decimal digits encoded as IA5 (the most common syntax in Europe, because X.400(84) requires it), a number encoded as a 16 bit unsigned integer (US GOSIP) and general hexadecimal. The US GOSIP number maps onto two octets, high order byte first.

It should be clean in the common case of an address with network addresses and no selectors, give special encodings for X.25(80) and TCP/IP networks, be extensible and be reasonably compact.
sections.eli5: The text format has to be able to write every possible address, keep the usual simple case tidy, and leave room for new kinds of address later.

sections.title: The String Syntax
sections.content:
A string has up to three selectors, each followed by a slash, and then a list of network addresses. The selectors appear in the order presentation, session, transport. You can leave out the leading ones: a transport selector alone is allowed, but a session selector needs a transport selector too. Several network addresses are joined with _.

A selector is written in one of four ways: a quoted IA5 string, a hash sign followed by decimal digits (US GOSIP), a hex string in quotes followed by H, or empty but present.

A network address has three forms. NS+ followed by dotted decimal or hex is the compact concrete binary form. The user oriented form is an afi, idi and optional dsp, where the afi is one of X121, DCC, TELEX, PSTN, ISDN, ICD or LOCAL. The third form is an idp digit string plus hex, for ISO 8348 compatibility. A dsp can be abstract decimal (d), abstract binary (x), local IA5 (l), or one of the special forms RFC-1006, X.25(80), ECMA-117-Binary and ECMA-117-Decimal.

The RFC-1006 form takes either a dotted-decimal IP address or a DNS domain name. The domain name is for convenient input. If it maps to several IP addresses, several network addresses should be generated. When converting an encoded address to a string, the IP address form should always be used.
sections.eli5: The address is written left to right: optional labels for the program, then the machine address itself. Several machine addresses can be joined with an underscore if one place has more than one.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives four examples, shown in the box below. The first has one transport selector and two network addresses. The second has all three selectors written in US GOSIP form, followed by an X.121 address. The third mixes a hex selector with a TELEX address that carries an X.25(80) part. The fourth is a bare RFC 1006 address with no selectors, which shows the clean common case.

Section 4 adds that, in the NS notation, the concrete binary form is given. Otherwise the notation represents the abstract syntax of a network address, which must be encoded according to Addendum 2 of ISO 8348.
sections.eli5: These are four sample addresses, from a very simple one to a longer one with every part filled in.

sections.title: Macros for Common Addresses
sections.content:
Some addresses are common enough to deserve a short name. If a network address parses as an otherstring, then =, then anything else, the leading string is treated as a macro and replaced by its value. Substitution may be applied recursively. When showing an address to a person, the longest available substitution should be used.

The RFC says no macro should ever be relied on, but suggests four standard ones: Int-X25(80), Janet-X25(80), Internet-RFC-1006 and IXI. Each expands to a TELEX prefix, followed by the X.25(80) or RFC-1006 part.
sections.eli5: A macro is a nickname for a long piece of an address. The computer swaps the nickname for the full text when it needs it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states only that security considerations are not discussed in the memo. The string format is a notation for people to read, so it defines no protections of its own.
sections.eli5: The memo does not talk about safety. It is only about how to write an address.
